strengths: Clear and well-written exposition of background (Stein-based control functionals, MLMC) and of the proposed method; the MLCF estimator is easy to understand and implement.

The proposed method is sensible: applying non-parametric Stein control functionals per level of the MLMC telescoping sum is a natural and potentially useful combination, and it is more broadly applicable than prior multilevel control variate methods tailored to specific PDEs or kernels.

The paper provides both an unbiasedness proof (Proposition 1) and a variance/convergence-rate analysis (Theorem 2), giving theoretical support for the claimed faster convergence rate when the integrand and density are smooth and dimension is moderate.

Empirical results on two differential-equation examples, including a real-data Bayesian inference task (Lotka-Volterra with the lynx-hare dataset), show MLCF outperforming MLMC and CF baselines under matched budgets, and demonstrate that QMC/LHS designs can further help.
Use of MCMC samples with unnormalized densities makes the method relevant to Bayesian inference practice.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a fairly mechanical combination of existing components (control functionals of Oates et al. 2017/2019 applied levelwise within the standard MLMC telescoping sum), and the theoretical result is essentially Theorem 1 of Oates et al. (2019) applied per level, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

The paper explicitly positions itself as an 'initial work' and defers a core component — optimal allocation of samples across levels — to a 'full version'. Since level allocation is central to MLMC efficiency, the submitted version feels incomplete.

Evaluation is narrow: only two examples (2D ODE, 8D Lotka-Volterra), no higher-dimensional or more challenging benchmarks, no comparison with other plausible baselines (e.g., multilevel Bayesian quadrature of Li et al. 2023 where feasible, or parametric Stein control variates), and no ablations on the choice of m_l vs n_l, kernel hyperparameters, or number of levels.

The variance bound in Theorem 2 is loose and not validated empirically (observed convergence rates are not compared to the predicted O(n^{-(τ/d)-1/2}) rates); moreover, the experiments violate some assumptions (as admitted in Appendix B), so the gap between theory and practice is not examined.

Several presentation issues: tables label level columns as 'l = 0, 1, 1'; figures are small and hard to read with no numerical summaries (e.g., median/RMSE tables); typos ('combing', 'Baysian', inconsistent naming 'multilevel control function'); only 2–6 samples at the top level in some settings raises questions about the reliability and practical stability of per-level control functional fits.
No discussion of code/release or reproducibility details beyond sparse appendix descriptions; kernel choices and tuning procedures for the Stein kernel in the posterior setting are under-specified.

strengths: The proposed MLCF estimator is well-motivated: combining Stein-based control functionals with the MLMC telescoping sum is a natural and practically relevant direction, and the method is genuinely more broadly applicable than prior multilevel control variate approaches (e.g., Nobile & Tesei 2015, Fairbanks et al. 2017).

The paper provides both an unbiased estimator (Proposition 1, with proof) and a variance/convergence-rate analysis (Theorem 2), and the theoretical result correctly identifies the dependence on smoothness and dimension.

The empirical evaluation covers both a synthetic ODE example and a real-data Bayesian inference task (Lotka-Volterra with the lynx-hare dataset), and compares against reasonable baselines (MLMC, CF, MCMC) and sample-design variants (QMC, LHS, IID).
Experimental details such as per-level costs and sample allocations are reported in Appendix B, which supports some reproducibility of the setup.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a direct, fairly mechanical combination of MLMC (Giles 2008/2015) with control functionals (Oates et al. 2017/2019). Theorem 2 is explicitly an adaptation of the proof of Theorem 1 of Oates et al. [2019] (with Wendland 2004), so the technical contribution beyond existing results is small.

The paper self-identifies as incomplete: the conclusion states 'In this initial work... In the full version of this paper we will consider the optimal sample size at each level.' Optimal sample allocation is central to MLMC performance and its absence substantially weakens both the method and the experiments.

Experimental validation is thin: only two low-dimensional (d = 2 and d = 8) examples, small sample budgets, and no comparison against the most relevant competing method, multilevel Bayesian quadrature (Li et al. 2023), even though the ODE example appears to be drawn from that paper's setting. The claim that other methods are 'very difficult or not feasible' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The theoretical convergence rate O(n^{(-τ/d)-1/2}) is not empirically verified: there are no experiments demonstrating the predicted rate or the dependence on τ and d, and Appendix B concedes that several assumptions (A1-A8) are violated in the tested settings, leaving the practical relevance of the theory unclear.

Presentation and rigor issues: convergence rate expressions contain apparent typos (e.g., O(n^{(-τ/d)-1/2}) instead of O(n^{-1/2-τ/d})); Tables 1 and 2 contain repeated column labels ('l = 1' twice); Equation (1) of the Stein kernel has an inconsistent index (k(x,y) vs k(x,x')); hyperparameter choices for the squared-exponential kernel (bandwidth, m_l/n_l ratio selection) are not described.

The variance bound treats levels independently and assumes sufficiently dense X_0^l with fill-distance O(m^{-1/d}), which is a strong requirement in higher dimensions; there is no discussion of how MLCF behaves when this fails or how the kernel choice interacts with the bound.
No code or supplementary implementation is provided, and reproducibility of the MCMC-based experiment (Stan configuration, chain settings, budget accounting) is insufficient.

For a top-tier venue, the significance is limited: this reads as a promising workshop-length contribution ('initial work') rather than a complete, competitive paper; the missing optimal-allocation analysis and narrow empirical scope are not offset by the incremental theoretical gain.

strengths: The core idea of applying non-parametric Stein-based control functionals (CF) at each level of an MLMC telescoping sum is natural and sensible, and yields a clean, easy-to-implement estimator (Proposition 1, Remark 1) that is unbiased and applicable to unnormalized densities arising in Bayesian inference.

The paper provides a theoretical variance/convergence-rate analysis (Theorem 2) showing that MLCF improves on the O(n^{-1/2}) MLMC rate under smoothness assumptions, giving the work some analytical grounding rather than being purely empirical.

Empirical evaluation includes a Bayesian inference task on a real ecological dataset (Lotka–Volterra / lynx–hare data) with MCMC samples, which is a relevant and realistic use case, and the ODE experiment sensibly compares QMC, LHS, and i.i.d. design choices for the design points.

The positioning against existing multilevel control-variate methods (Nobile & Tesei 2015, Fairbanks et al. 2017, Geraci et al. 2017, multilevel BQ) is reasonable: these are indeed tailored to specific problem classes, whereas MLCF is generic.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is a direct composition of two existing techniques (MLMC of Giles 2008/2015 and control functionals of Oates et al. 2017/2019). Theorem 2 is an explicit adaptation of Theorem 1 of Oates et al. [2019] to the telescoping setting, and the proof is a short, routine extension. The conceptual contribution is thin for a top-tier venue.

The key practical ingredient of MLMC — optimal allocation of the sample budget across levels — is explicitly deferred to a 'full version of this paper.' Since the performance of the estimator depends heavily on the choice of (m_l, n_l), the submitted version is an incomplete contribution, and the reported results may not reflect the method's best (or fair) operating regime.

Evaluation is narrow and possibly unfair/unclear: only two low-dimensional examples (2D and 8D) are considered; sample sizes in Tables 1–2 appear hand-picked or borrowed from MLMC's optimal allocation; there is no comparison against the closest related method, multilevel Bayesian quadrature (Li et al., 2023), despite it being discussed in the introduction; and the accounting of the CF O(m^3) cost and of Stein-kernel construction time in the budget-constrained comparisons is not transparent.

The theoretical rate relies on strong assumptions (A5 boundary condition, A8 fill-distance h_l ≤ q m_l^{-1/d}) that are hard to verify in practice, and the appendix concedes that the assumptions 'are not fulfilled' in the experiments, so the fast convergence rate is never empirically validated against the theory. With m_l as small as 2–6 at high levels (Tables 1–2), the fill-distance assumption is implausible.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top-tier conference: Figures 1–2 are illegible at the rendered size (axes, legends, and box plots cannot be read reliably); Tables 1 and 2 contain duplicated column headers ('l = 0 l = 1 l = 1'); and there are multiple typos ('MCLF', 'Baysian', 'to simply the equations', 'combing the bound', 'multilevel control function'), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully prepared.

The claimed 'widely applicable' property is asserted rather than demonstrated: no scaling study in dimension, no experiments where the method is compared in higher d, and the restriction that the log-density gradient must be evaluated pointwise is not discussed in terms of cost or feasibility for challenging posteriors.

Missing ablations and details: no sensitivity analysis of kernel choice/hyperparameters for the Stein kernel, no investigation of how performance depends on m_l/n_l or the number of levels L, and no reporting of uncertainty in the budget accounting. Reproducibility is limited since no code or complete experimental specification is provided.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap: MLMC uses low-fidelity models as raw control variates without optimizing the control variate itself, and existing Stein-based CVs ignore multilevel structure. The proposed MLCF combines these two lines of work in a natural and broadly applicable way, with the ability to handle unnormalized densities common in Bayesian inference.

Theoretical analysis is provided and appears sound: unbiasedness (Prop 3.1), variance bounds (Thm 3.2, extending Oates et al. 2019), optimal sample allocation under cost constraints (Thm 3.3), and a combined rate that improves on MLMC's O(n^{-1/2}) when smoothness is high and dimension is low/moderate. Proofs in the appendix are complete and the Lagrange-multiplier allocation derivation is correct.

The extension to variational inference (MLCFRG, Prop 3.4) is interesting: it recycles previous-iteration gradients à la Fujisawa & Sato (2021) but with control functionals, reducing cost to O(dn_L^3) and yielding a useful simplified update rule.

Empirical evaluation covers several distinct settings: a synthetic example validating the optimal allocation, a boundary-value ODE with QMC/LHS/IID design comparisons, Bayesian inference on the real-world Lotka-Volterra (lynx-hare) data with MCMC samples, and BNN variational inference with ablations on kernels and sample sizes. MLCF consistently outperforms MLMC and CF under matched budgets.

The paper is honest about limitations (cubic kernel cost, dependence on fidelity hierarchies, curse of dimensionality) and includes practical guidance (hyperparameter selection via marginal likelihood, kernel derivatives in the appendix) that supports reproducibility and adoption.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is a fairly natural composition of two established ideas: applying control functionals (Oates et al. 2017/2019) level-wise within an MLMC telescoping sum (Giles 2008). The theory largely adapts Theorem 1 of Oates et al. (2019) with the standard MLMC cost-allocation optimization; the comparison B_MLCF < B_CF is a heuristic case analysis rather than a clean theorem. Novelty is solid but incremental.

The theoretical assumptions are restrictive and only partially satisfied by the experiments: A7 requires the integrand increments to lie in a specific RKHS, A8 requires quasi-uniform design points at construction locations (satisfied by space-filling designs, but at odds with the MCMC-sample setting of the Lotka-Volterra experiment), and the favorable rate O(n^{-(τ/d)-1/2}) degrades quickly with dimension. The paper itself concedes in Appendix D that some assumptions are not fulfilled in its own experiments, leaving a theory–practice gap.

The empirical scope is modest: small dimensions (d≤8 for inference, d=2 for the ODE), one real dataset, small BNNs on a single subsampled UCI dataset. The claims that competing multilevel-CV methods (Li et al. 2023, Nobile & Tesei 2015, etc.) are infeasible in these settings are asserted but not empirically verified against any of them.

In the BNN experiments, MLCFRG uses 1 MC sample while baselines use 5; the compute-matched fairness of this comparison is not rigorously established (kernel cost is discounted as negligible, which holds for small nets but may not hold generally).
No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility given the implementation subtleties (per-level kernel tuning, simplified vs. unbiased estimator, kernel hyperparameter selection).

Presentation issues: inconsistent labeling (Proposition 3.1 referred to as 'Theorem 3.1'; Theorem 3.4 stated as a proposition), typos ('MCLF', 'combing', 'simplier', 'Variation Inference'), and some hand-wavy passages (e.g., the RKHS-norm estimation discussion in Section 3).

strengths: The core idea is sensible and clearly motivated: treating low-fidelity models in MLMC as 'imperfect' control variates and then applying non-parametric Stein-based control functionals on top of the level differences is a natural and clean combination of two established lines of work.

The estimator is unbiased, and the paper provides a complete theoretical package: variance bounds (Theorem 3.2), optimal sample allocation across levels (Theorem 3.3), and a corresponding budget-dependent bound (Eq. 7), with full proofs in the appendix.

The extension to variational inference (MLCFRG) is a nice bonus, including a simplified SGD update (Prop 3.4) with reduced computational/memory cost, connecting to the MLMRG framework of Fujisawa and Sato (2021).

Experiments cover a range of settings (synthetic RKHS example, boundary-value ODE, Lotka-Volterra Bayesian inference with real data, BNN VI), and MLCF consistently improves over MLMC and CF baselines under matched budgets. Practical details (kernel selection, hyperparameter tuning via marginal likelihood, QMC/LHS designs) are provided and improve reproducibility.
Limitations are acknowledged candidly (cubic kernel cost, smoothness/dimension dependence, need for a fidelity hierarchy), and several future directions are discussed.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the contribution is essentially a straightforward composition of two well-known techniques — MLMC (Giles 2008/2015) and control functionals (Oates et al. 2017/2019). The variance bound in Theorem 3.2 is a direct adaptation of Theorem 1 of Oates et al. (2019) applied level-wise, and the optimal allocation in Theorem 3.3 follows the standard Giles derivation with an adjusted variance surrogate. A reviewer familiar with both literatures can anticipate almost every result.

Severe restrictions on practical applicability: the fast convergence rate requires low-to-moderate dimension, smooth integrands and density, quasi-uniform design points (A8), and score function availability. All experiments are in dimension d ≤ 8; there is no evidence the method helps in the high-dimensional regimes where ML variance reduction matters most. The authors also admit that several assumptions (e.g., A5, A8) are not fulfilled in their own experiments, which weakens the link between theory and practice.

The variance guarantees are for an upper bound that depends on RKHS norms ||f_l - f_{l-1}||_{H_l+} and constants r_l that are unknown in general; the discussion of data-driven estimation of these norms is deferred to citations rather than developed or validated. The theoretical optimal allocation (Theorem 3.3) is only used in one synthetic example where the norms are computable by construction — arguably a circular evaluation, and there the MLMC allocation actually performs comparably or better at small budgets (Fig. 2), which undercuts the practical value of the theory.

The experimental comparisons are somewhat favorable by construction: in several examples the alternative multilevel CV approaches (Li et al. 2023; Nobile and Tesei 2015; Fairbanks et al. 2017) are dismissed as infeasible rather than compared. For the BNN experiments, MLCFRG uses 1 Monte Carlo sample while baselines use 5, and the overall computational accounting (including the O(m^3) Gram inversion and score evaluations) is not carefully matched, making the cost-effectiveness claims hard to verify.

The VI extension inherits assumptions that are unlikely to hold (RKHS membership of gradient functions, Stein kernel conditions on the variational distribution at every iteration), and the variance bound in Prop 3.4 is only conditional on λ_L − λ_{L-1}; no convergence analysis of the resulting optimization scheme is given. Results are limited to a single dataset (wine-quality) and small networks.

Presentation issues reduce polish: naming inconsistencies between 'Theorem 3.1' and 'Proposition 3.1', multiple typos ('combing', 'simplier', 'as we shown', 'would not be an severe issue'), and occasionally confusing derivations (e.g., the B.4 derivation mixes r_l and a uniform bound r mid-computation without clear justification). The rate comparison O(n^{(-τ/d)-1/2}) vs O(n^{-1/2}) is stated loosely without clarifying the τ regimes where the gain is meaningful.

strengths: The proposed MLCF estimator is a natural but well-executed combination of two mature lines of work (Stein-based control functionals and multilevel Monte Carlo), and the paper clearly identifies the gap: MLMC does not minimize the variance of level differences, while CV methods do not exploit the fidelity hierarchy.

The theoretical contribution is substantive: unbiasedness (Prop 3.1), a variance upper bound with a faster convergence rate than standard MLMC under smoothness assumptions (Theorem 3.2), and closed-form optimal sample allocation across levels with a budget constraint (Theorem 3.3), with proofs provided in the appendix.

The extension to variational inference (MLCFRG, Prop 3.4) is a nice addition that reduces the computational/memory cost relative to applying CF at every level, and connects the method to machine learning applications.

Experiments cover a reasonably diverse set of settings: a synthetic example validating the sample-size theory, a boundary-value ODE with QMC/LHS designs, Bayesian inference for Lotka-Volterra with unnormalized posteriors and MCMC samples, and BNN variational inference with ablations over kernels and sample sizes.

The paper is honest about limitations (cubic kernel cost, smoothness dependence, need for a fidelity hierarchy) and provides practical guidance on hyperparameter selection and the simplified biased estimator.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core construction is essentially applying the existing control functional estimator (Oates et al., 2017, 2019) to each level of the standard MLMC telescoping sum, and the variance analysis is a direct adaptation of Theorem 1 of Oates et al. (2019). The contribution is an extension rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The assumptions are strong and limit practical applicability: A8 requires quasi-uniform design points X0 at each level, which conflicts with the MCMC-sample setting emphasized for Bayesian inference; the authors themselves acknowledge (Appendix D) that assumptions are not fulfilled in the main experiments, creating a theory-practice gap. The claimed faster rate O(n^{-(tau/d)-1/2}) degrades quickly with dimension, restricting impact to low/moderate dimensions as the paper concedes.
The comparison B_MLCF < B_CF is only an informal case analysis of upper bounds, not a theorem; upper-bound comparisons can be loose and the actual variance ordering is not guaranteed.

The optimal sample sizes in Theorem 3.3 require RKHS norms ||f_l - f_{l-1}|| and constants r_l that are generally unavailable in practice; the paper's suggestion to estimate RKHS norms from data is only sketched with pointers to other works, and the synthetic experiment exploits closed-form norms.

Scalability concerns are underexplored: all experiments are low-dimensional (d=2 ODE, 8-dim Lotka-Volterra, ~400-500 parameter BNNs) with cubic kernel costs; no experiment probes where the method breaks down, and no strong modern baselines (e.g., random-feature/neural Stein CVs, Sard-based semi-exact CVs) are compared empirically.

The BNN experiments are somewhat confounded: MLCFRG uses 1 MC sample per gradient while baselines use 5, and only one dataset (UCI wine-quality-red) with small models is tested; improvements in ELBO convergence could partly reflect per-iteration compute differences.

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies ('as we shown', 'MCLF', 'simplier', 'not an severe issue', Proposition vs. 'Theorem 3.1' naming inconsistency, y-coordinate typo in Equation (10)); Figures 5-9 are hard to read due to overlapping curves and no quantitative tables.
No statement about code release, which weakens reproducibility for a method with many implementation details (kernel choice, hyperparameter tuning, sample splitting).
